chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
title: Getting the job at the Benjamin Harrison club and the flood
summary: A pianist friend of Harry's heard her; a flood stranded them downtown and Xavier Cugat was in town.

blocks.x: I don't remember if you talked on our tape about how you came to work at the B.H.L. It's certainly on the interview with Louis McMill an. Can you go over it one more time?

MS. SULLIVAN: Well, Jenny Dilliard, this

pianist, she was a friend of Harry's and she had heard me sing around, probably around the house. See Harry and the boys used to, at times, rehearse at home and they would bring people like Jenny and some of their colleagues, some of the entertainers around, and they would have parties at the house and they had heard me sing. So when Jenny got this job at the Benjamin, Harris, and Literary Club which is 966 Liberty Avenue in downtown Pittsburgh. A very small club, an after-hours club. And so she got in touch with me and told me to go down and audition. So this was the beginning of 1936, so by this time I had managed to get a little gig out in East Liberty. A gig is a one-night stand. And so I went up on the hill up to the Crawford Grill to see some of the musicians when I got through work and to find out how to get downtown to 966 Liberty Avenue. I didn't want to have to go down there and start looking up at the buildings to find out where I was going. So anyway, one of the musicians said, I'll take you down there as far as I can but don't look now, there's a flood going on. So we got in the car and drove down Wylie Avenue,
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

and just at the foot of Wyle Avenue the water was coming up very fast and I would say that at the foot of Wyle Avenue, by this time, the water might have been up to maybe the first story of some of the stores downtown. And so that went that audition. The water, that flood, got up to about eighteen inches below the ceiling of the club where I was supposed to audition and the club was on the second floor so you can imagine what a flood that was.
In fact, it was quite a flood. We were stranded around there, the locality there for weeks without lights, without food, well, whatever food we had.

And Xavier Cugat's band was on the stage in one of the theatres and all his instruments got wet, got washed off the stage. It was quite a flood. And I really didn't get to audition again until June of that year. The flood was March 17, 1936. So by the time they cleaned up downtown and they got everything restored, back to normal again, I auditioned at the club and I went to work. They had another girl singing there and I was on trial for a week. We were making fourteen dollars a week on tips, and of course Jenny was on piano.
